bears.note: The Q1 thesis was the first of the thirteen condemned theses.

rel.basis: Copenhaver's report of Pico's own account of the 'usual approach' (Scotus, Bonaventura, the Scotists and nominalists, and Thomas as Pico read him) gives the authorities behind the position Edelheit reports Pico adopting on operation over substance.

quotes.t: Pico added it to part of the thesis because he disagreed, to some extent, not just with Aquinas but also with Scotus and the others: he saw all their views on a relevant issue—locating angels in space and time—as largely …

quotes.t: Discovering and promoting agreement among famously opposed authorities was one of two grand schemes floated by the Conclusions. The other was a truly thunderous innovation: urging Christians to be saved by Jewish mysticism—Kabbalah. But Kabbalah was not on the table …

rel.basis: Copenhaver names agreement among opposed authorities as one of the two grand schemes of the Conclusions, bearing out Still's point that the concord theme is announced in the theses as well as in De ente.

judged.justification: Records that Q1 contains no Platonist or Dionysian sources.

quotes.t: Likewise prominent in Q1, though absent from the Conclusions, were Durand and Étienne Tempier. Thirteen others mentioned less often in Q1 but not at all in the Conclusions were Anselm of Aosta, Landolfo Caracciolo, Bernard de Gannat, Bonaventura, Jean Cabrol, …

One influential referee of scholastic disputes entered the Q1 conversation not under his name but as an anonymous authority behind an explosive document. He was Étienne Tempier, the Bishop of Paris in 1277. In that year the Bishop

condemned more than two hundred “detestable errors” based on “writings by pagans” that he linked with “students of the arts in Paris.” Tempier’s backers were theologians worried about Aristotelian natural philosophy as interpreted by Averroes and other Muslims

bears.note: Pico's judges used the Paris articles against him.

quotes.t: Several articles on Tempier’s list mentioned angels. These spirits had fascinated Christians ever since the Gospels reported Gabriel’s annunciation to Mary, a scene depicted in countless works of art.

How could Gabriel, without a body, go there or anywhere? One response was that “separated substances”—spirits without bodies, like angels—can be somewhere through what they do there: in effect—as Thomas said—after being in one place (Heaven), they can be in …

warrants.t: Copenhaver cites Aquinas, Summa theologiae 3.52.2 in his note; the passage itself is not quoted in the text.
warrants.q: after being in one place (Heaven), they can be in another place (Mary’s room) by doing something there

judged.justification: States the 'operational' account of angelic location that Q1 leans on.

quotes.t: Such puzzles of placement interested Godfrey of Fontaines, who died around 1309. He was a Belgian who studied with Henry of Ghent but followed Aquinas as much as Henry. Examining the 1277 statements on locating angels, Godfrey concluded that “they …

rel.basis: Copenhaver reports Pico citing Godfrey of Fontaines that the 1277 Paris articles are internally inconsistent and need correction, to discredit their authority; Edelheit reports Garsia using those same 1277 articles as a valid criterion for condemning Pico's view, the opposite assessment of the articles' authority.

judged.justification: Shows Pico's use of Godfrey to blunt the 1277 articles that his judges used.

quotes.t: In a quodlibetal question where Godfrey dealt with angels, he also produced a manifesto that could have taught Pico about the benefits of disagreement:

When an issue is so unsettled by lack of certainty . . . that beliefs about it may vary—without risk to faith and morals and without rash claims for either position—then, to tie things up with a chain that holds …

Godfrey wrote these stirring words—easy to mistake for a call to enlightenment—in response to disagreements about angels. He argued for open debate, yes, but debate open in the scholastic way, where fides always came first in the fides quaerens intellectum …

judged.justification: Shows a defence of disputation that arose from the angel debate.

quotes.t: Why should Pico have cared about what Godfrey thought about what the Bishop of Paris said about angels? The prince’s problem in Q1 was the Harrowing of Hell, where no unfallen angels were found, only devils. But

he remembered “scriptural texts that seem to give angels a place by describing them as . . . sent to one place or another”—like Gabriel visiting Mary or angels climbing Jacob’s ladder or heavenly spirits leading Moses and his troops …

rel.basis: Copenhaver's account of Pico's scriptural reasoning (angels act here or there, not that they are strictly in a place) and Edelheit's account of Pico's scholastic reasoning (presence identified with operation) describe the same doctrine from two of Pico's own arguments.

judged.justification: Explains why an angel-location dispute sits inside the Q1 defence of a Christological thesis.

quotes.t: Pico shifted the conversation from Hell to heavenly messengers after just a few paragraphs of Q1. He did not call attention to this transition, whose motives—prophylactic and practical—are easy to imagine.
First, in a spasm of caution, he may have worried that Christ was a riskier topic than angels.

Christ’s soul in Hell, as scholastic theologians described it, was a “separated substance”—separated from his body. But angels, pure spirits without bodies, were also treated as separated substances. Hence, angels were safer substitutes for Christ in Pico’s metaphysical inquiry.
Pico studied the localization of angels in order to understand how Christ’s soul could have been located in Hell.

warrants.t: Copenhaver infers Pico's motives; he notes that Cabrol's index has eight columns under angelus but only half a column under infernus.

open.t: Pico's own motive for the shift from Hell to angels is not stated by him; Copenhaver calls the motives 'easy to imagine'.

rel.basis: Copenhaver's inference that Pico shifted from Hell to angels for prophylactic and practical reasons is the reason he gives, elsewhere, for treating angels as surrogates for the harder, less examinable problem of Christ's bodiless presence.

judged.justification: Explains why angelology fills the defence of the Q1 thesis.

quotes.t: From Pico’s perspective, the placement of bodiless angels and souls was of great interest for at least five of his theses—on the eucharist, the incarnation and the descent clause in the Creed.

judged.justification: Extends angel-location beyond Q1 to five theses.

The terminology had evolved to explicate a passage from Peter Lombard’s Sentences: There are two ways for scripture to say that something is or is not in a place or enclosable (circumscriptibile), either because it produces distance in a place …

warrants.t: Copenhaver quotes Lombard, Sent. 1.37.6.1 in translation.
warrants.q: There are two ways for scripture to say that something is or is not in a place or enclosable

quotes.t: If so, an angel could be somewhere, in or at a place, and yet some insisted that angels could have places “only by activity.” Others countered that if an angel happened not to act somewhere, it would be nowhere: angels …

Pico investigated all this and considered the possibility that “a bodiless substance . . . should by no means have a place.” His conclusion, however, was that a separated substance . . . is indeed present as to place by …
so it was befitting for Christ’s soul to have been in Hell—where I believe it was—only by the effect and by acting. . . . The basis for the presence of Christ’s soul was what he did there.

rel.basis: Edelheit and Copenhaver both report Pico's conclusion that an incorporeal substance is present in a place definitively (by delimitation), not by its substance but by its operation or effect, agreeing with Scotus on the mode of presence.

Copenhaver states simply that Pico's conclusion agrees with Scotus and the Scotists; Edelheit, reporting Garsia's five-way taxonomy, places Pico's actual position as a distinct fifth view, not simply identical to the Scotist first view, which narrows Copenhaver's simpler equation.

judged.justification: Shows the Q1 thesis rests on an angelology of presence by delimitation and effect.

quotes.t: No: under interrogation he insisted that “no one should understand me to say that Christ’s soul did not descend into Hell.” His judges, nonetheless, ruled that the Q1 thesis strictly speaking (secundum rigorem sermonis) and given the meaning of the …
The interrogators recorded their obdurate verdict on March 5, 1487—before the Apology was written, of course.
Thomas also taught that Jesus went to Hell both essentially and effectively, with different effects for different locations.

Where the damned were imprisoned, one effect was “to silence their disbelief and malice,” while elsewhere the Lord “shed the light of eternal glory on the blessed Fathers kept in Hell only because of original sin.” Moreover, Jesus was essentially …
“while remaining in one part of Hell”—the escapable part—“he distributed his effect to all the parts.”
But how could a disembodied soul go to a place—one district of Hell rather than another? Related questions applied to all the damned souls, whose bones were moldering in their graves.
If this was a Christian’s only instruction, that Christ “descended to Hell,” what else was a believer obliged to believe about the descent? This question was at the heart of Pico’s defense in Q1.
